goals: Name alkenes and describe the sigma and pi bonds and sp² hybridisation of ethene
Identify structural and geometrical isomers of alkenes

slides.heading: Alkenes: hydrocarbons with a C=C bond
slides.body_md: **Alkenes** are unsaturated hydrocarbons that contain **one carbon–carbon double bond**; general formula **CₙH₂ₙ**. They are also called **olefins** ("oil-forming"). The double bond makes them far more reactive than alkanes.

visual.alt: Table of the first five alkenes with formula, boiling point in degrees Celsius and state at 298 kelvin

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on alkenes. Alkenes are hydrocarbons with one carbon carbon double bond, and their general formula is C n H two n. They are unsaturated, which makes them much more reactive than alkanes. The first three members are gases at room temperature, and the next members are liquids. In this part we study their structure, naming, isomerism, preparation and physical properties.

slides.heading: Naming alkenes
slides.body_md: (1) Choose the **longest chain that contains the double bond**; change **-ane to -ene**. (2) Number from the end that gives the **double bond the lowest locant**. (3) Write the locant before "-ene" (but-1-ene, pent-2-ene). (4) Name and number the substituents as for alkanes. (5) Add **cis** or **trans** where it applies. For two double bonds use **-diene**.

visual.alt: Table of six alkenes with their structural formula and IUPAC name

slides.narration: To name an alkene, take the longest chain that includes the double bond and change the ending from ane to ene. Number the chain from the end that gives the double bond the lowest number, and write that number before the ending. So the four carbon alkene with the bond at the end is but one ene, and with the bond in the middle is but two ene. Substituents are named and numbered as in alkanes.

slides.heading: Structure of the double bond in ethene
slides.body_md: Each carbon of ethene is **sp² hybridised**: three sp² orbitals form σ bonds (one C–C, two C–H) in one plane at about **120°** (H–C–H 117°, H–C=C 121.5°). The leftover **p orbitals** overlap **sideways** to form the **π bond**, with its electron cloud above and below the plane. **C=C is 134 pm** (shorter than C–C, 154 pm) and ethene has **5 σ bonds and 1 π bond**.

slides.narration: In ethene each carbon atom is sp two hybridised. The three hybrid orbitals make sigma bonds, one to the other carbon and two to hydrogen, all lying in one plane with bond angles close to one hundred and twenty degrees. The unhybridised p orbitals on the two carbons overlap sideways to form a pi bond, whose electron cloud lies above and below the plane. The carbon carbon bond is one hundred and thirty four picometres long.

slides.heading: Isomerism in alkenes
slides.body_md: Alkenes show **chain isomerism** (but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene), **position isomerism** (but-1-ene and but-2-ene) and **geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism**, which needs **two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon**. C₄H₈ has 3 alkenes (4 stereoisomers); C₅H₁₀ has 5 alkenes (6 stereoisomers). Alkenes are also **functional isomers of cycloalkanes** (C₄H₈: cyclobutane).

slides.narration: Alkenes show several kinds of isomerism. Butene with the bond at the end and two methylpropene are chain isomers. Butene with the bond at the end and butene with the bond in the middle are position isomers. Only but two ene has two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon, so only it has cis and trans forms. Alkenes are also functional isomers of cycloalkanes with the same formula.

slides.heading: Preparation of alkenes: the main routes
slides.body_md: Alkenes are made by **dehydration of alcohols**, **dehydrohalogenation** of alkyl halides, **dehalogenation of vicinal dihalides** with zinc, **Kolbe electrolysis** of potassium salts of dicarboxylic acids, and **partial reduction of alkynes**.

visual.alt: Table of five preparations of alkenes with reagents and examples

slides.narration: Here are the main ways of preparing alkenes. Alcohols lose water when heated with concentrated sulphuric acid. Alkyl halides lose hydrogen halide with alcoholic potassium hydroxide. A vicinal dihalide loses two halogen atoms with zinc dust. Potassium succinate gives ethene on electrolysis. And an alkyne can be partly reduced, to a cis alkene with Lindlar catalyst or to a trans alkene with sodium in liquid ammonia.

slides.heading: Dehydrohalogenation and Saytzeff's rule
slides.body_md: Alcoholic KOH removes H and X from adjacent carbons ($\ce{CH3CH2Br + KOH -> CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O}$). When more than one alkene can form, **Saytzeff's rule** says the **more substituted** (more stable) alkene is the **major product**; the H is taken from the β-carbon with **fewer hydrogens**.

slides.narration: In dehydrohalogenation, alcoholic potassium hydroxide removes a hydrogen and a halogen from neighbouring carbons. If two alkenes are possible, Saytzeff rule tells us the more substituted alkene is the major product. With two bromobutane, hydrogen can leave from carbon three or carbon one. Loss from carbon three gives but two ene, which has two alkyl groups on the double bond and is more stable, so it is the main product.

slides.heading: Worked example: applying Saytzeff's rule
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is heated with alcoholic KOH. Name the major and minor alkenes.

**Solution.** The carbon bearing Br is C-2, with β-carbons C-1 (three H, in a CH₃ group) and C-3 (two H, in CH₂). Loss of H from C-3 gives **2-methylbut-2-ene**, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, with **three** alkyl groups on C=C: **major**. Loss from C-1 gives **2-methylbut-1-ene**, CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, with two: **minor**.

visual.alt: Table comparing 2-methylbut-2-ene and 2-methylbut-1-ene by number of alkyl groups on the double bond and their role as major or minor product

slides.narration: Find the carbon with the halogen, then look at the neighbouring carbons. Two methyl butane with bromine on carbon two can lose hydrogen from carbon one, in a methyl group, or from carbon three. Loss from carbon three gives two methylbut two ene, with three alkyl groups on the double bond. That is the more stable alkene and the major product. Loss from carbon one gives two methylbut one ene, the minor product.

slides.heading: Dehydration of alcohols
slides.body_md: Heating an alcohol with **concentrated H₂SO₄ at 443 K** removes water from adjacent carbons ($\ce{CH3CH2OH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O}$). At a lower temperature (413 K) with excess alcohol an **ether** forms instead. The ease of dehydration is **3° > 2° > 1°** (the order of carbocation stability), and the Saytzeff product predominates.

visual.alt: Dehydration of ethanol with concentrated sulfuric acid at 443 kelvin gives ethene and water
visual.caption: Ethanol to ethene

slides.narration: When ethanol is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid at four hundred and forty three kelvin, a molecule of water is removed from adjacent carbons and ethene is formed. At a lower temperature and with excess alcohol, an ether forms instead, so the temperature must be controlled. Tertiary alcohols dehydrate most easily, then secondary, then primary, following the stability of the carbocation intermediate.

slides.heading: Other preparations: dihalides, Kolbe and alkynes
slides.body_md: **Vicinal dihalide:** $\ce{CH2BrCH2Br + Zn -> CH2=CH2 + ZnBr2}$. **Kolbe:** electrolysis of aqueous potassium succinate gives ethene (with CO₂, H₂ and KOH). **Alkynes:** hydrogen over **Lindlar's catalyst** (Pd on CaCO₃, poisoned) gives the **cis** alkene; **Na in liquid NH₃** gives the **trans** alkene.

visual.alt: Zinc removes two bromine atoms from 1,2-dibromoethane to give ethene and zinc bromide
visual.caption: Dehalogenation of a vicinal dibromide

slides.narration: Three more routes. A vicinal dibromide, with a bromine on each of two neighbouring carbons, loses both with zinc dust to give an alkene. In Kolbe electrolysis of aqueous potassium succinate, ethene forms at the anode. And alkynes can be reduced to alkenes: hydrogen with Lindlar catalyst gives the cis alkene, while sodium in liquid ammonia gives the trans alkene.

slides.heading: Worked example: cis or trans?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** How can pent-2-yne be converted into (a) cis-pent-2-ene and (b) trans-pent-2-ene?

**Solution.** (a) $\ce{CH3C#CCH2CH3 + H2 ->[Lindlar] CH3CH=CHCH2CH3}$ (Lindlar catalyst, Pd on CaCO₃, poisoned: both H add on the same face, giving the cis isomer). (b) Sodium in liquid ammonia adds the two H atoms on opposite faces (anti addition) to give **trans-pent-2-ene**.

visual.alt: Table of reagents for converting pent-2-yne into cis-pent-2-ene and trans-pent-2-ene

slides.narration: The choice of reagent decides the geometry of the alkene. Pent two yne with hydrogen over Lindlar catalyst, which is palladium on calcium carbonate poisoned to stop further reduction, adds both hydrogens on the same side and gives the cis alkene. Sodium in liquid ammonia adds the hydrogens on opposite sides and gives the trans alkene.

slides.heading: Physical properties of alkenes
slides.body_md: Alkenes are **non-polar or weakly polar**, so they are **insoluble in water** but soluble in organic solvents, **less dense than water**, with boiling points close to those of alkanes with the same carbon number (C₂–C₄ gases; C₅ onwards liquids). The boiling point rises with chain length and falls with branching. **cis** isomers are slightly polar and boil higher; **trans** isomers are more symmetrical and melt higher.

visual.alt: Table comparing boiling points, melting points and dipole moments of cis and trans isomers of but-2-ene and 1,2-dichloroethene

slides.narration: Alkenes are non polar or only weakly polar. They do not dissolve in water, but dissolve in organic solvents, and they are less dense than water. The boiling points are close to those of the alkanes with the same number of carbons. In cis isomers the bond dipoles add up, so the cis form is polar and boils higher. The trans form is symmetrical, has zero dipole moment, and fits better in a crystal, so it melts higher.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1

Cis isomers are polar and boil higher; trans isomers are symmetrical and melt higher.

visual.alt: Summary table of preparations of alkenes and their key reagents

slides.narration: To sum up Part one. Alkenes have the formula C n H two n and one sp two carbon double bond, made of one sigma and one pi bond. They show chain, position and geometrical isomerism. They are prepared by dehydration of alcohols, dehydrohalogenation following Saytzeff rule, dehalogenation of dihalides with zinc, Kolbe electrolysis, and partial reduction of alkynes. Cis isomers are polar and boil higher.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: In names, the double bond gets the lowest locant, even before substituents.

goals: Write the products of addition of H₂, X₂, HX, H₂SO₄ and H₂O to alkenes
Explain electrophilic addition with carbocations, Markownikoff's rule and the peroxide effect

slides.heading: Why alkenes undergo addition
slides.body_md: The **π bond** is weaker (about 270 kJ mol⁻¹) than the σ bond (about 350 kJ mol⁻¹) and its electrons are exposed above and below the molecule, so alkenes are attacked by **electrophiles**. In an **addition reaction** the π bond breaks and two new σ bonds form: C=C + X–Y → X–C–C–Y.

visual.alt: Table of addition reagents and the product obtained from ethene

slides.narration: Alkenes are reactive because the pi bond is weaker than a sigma bond and its electrons are exposed above and below the molecule. Attacking species that seek electrons, called electrophiles, add to the double bond. In an addition reaction the pi bond breaks and two new sigma bonds form. In this part we study the addition of hydrogen, halogens, hydrogen halides, sulphuric acid and water.

slides.heading: Addition of hydrogen and halogens
slides.body_md: **Hydrogenation:** alkene + H₂ with finely divided Ni (473 K) or Pt/Pd (room temperature) gives the alkane. **Halogens:** Br₂ in CCl₄ or Cl₂ adds to give a **vicinal dihalide**; the **red-brown bromine colour is lost**, a test for unsaturation. Iodine adds poorly; fluorine reacts violently.

visual.alt: Ethene plus bromine gives 1,2-dibromoethane
visual.caption: Bromine is decolourised: test for a C=C bond

slides.narration: With hydrogen and a nickel catalyst at about four hundred and seventy three kelvin, an alkene is converted to the alkane. Halogens add across the double bond too. When ethene is passed into a solution of bromine in tetrachloromethane, the red brown colour disappears and colourless one two dibromoethane forms. This decolourisation is used as a test for a carbon carbon double bond.

slides.heading: Addition of HX and Markownikoff's rule
slides.body_md: Ethene + HBr → bromoethane. With **unsymmetrical alkenes**, **Markownikoff's rule**: *the negative part of the reagent adds to the carbon with fewer hydrogens* (equivalently, the H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens). So propene + HBr gives mainly **2-bromopropane**.

visual.alt: Table of three unsymmetrical alkenes, the hydrogen halide added and the major Markownikoff product

slides.narration: When a hydrogen halide adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, two products are possible, and Markownikoff rule tells us which is major. The negative part of the reagent goes to the carbon with fewer hydrogens. Propene with hydrogen bromide gives mainly two bromopropane, not one bromopropane. Two methylpropene with hydrogen bromide gives the tertiary bromide.

slides.heading: Mechanism: electrophilic addition of HBr to propene
slides.body_md: **Step 1 (slow):** the π electrons attack H⁺ of H–Br; H bonds to C-1 and the **carbocation** forms on C-2. **Step 2 (fast):** Br⁻ attacks the carbocation. The more stable **secondary** carbocation is formed in preference to the primary one, which explains Markownikoff's rule.

slides.narration: Here is the mechanism. In step one, the pi electrons of propene attack the hydrogen of hydrogen bromide. The hydrogen bonds to carbon one, the bromine leaves as a bromide ion, and a carbocation forms on carbon two. This step is slow. In step two, the bromide ion quickly attacks the positive carbon and two bromopropane forms. The secondary carbocation is favoured because it is more stable than the primary one.

slides.heading: Stability of carbocations
slides.body_md: Alkyl groups release electrons (**+I effect**) and their C–H bonds overlap with the empty p orbital (**hyperconjugation**), spreading the charge. So the stability order is **tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl**. The number of hyperconjugating C–H bonds is 9 for (CH₃)₃C⁺, 6 for (CH₃)₂CH⁺, 3 for CH₃CH₂⁺ and 0 for CH₃⁺.

visual.alt: Table of carbocations by type with the number of hyperconjugating C–H bonds and relative stability

slides.narration: The stability of carbocations explains Markownikoff rule. Alkyl groups push electrons towards the positive carbon, and their carbon hydrogen bonds can overlap with the empty p orbital, which is called hyperconjugation. The more alkyl groups, the more the charge is spread out. So a tertiary carbocation is the most stable, then secondary, then primary, and the methyl cation is the least stable.

slides.heading: Quick check: Markownikoff's rule
slides.body_md: Decide where H and Br add on an unsymmetrical alkene.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the hydrogens on each doubly bonded carbon, and add the negative part of the reagent to the carbon with fewer hydrogens.

slides.heading: Peroxide effect: anti-Markownikoff addition of HBr
slides.body_md: In the presence of a **peroxide** (benzoyl peroxide) HBr adds by a **free-radical chain** and the orientation reverses: propene gives **1-bromopropane**. Br• adds first to the carbon with more hydrogens, giving the more stable **secondary radical**. The effect is seen **only with HBr**; HCl (H–Cl too strong) and HI (I• unreactive) do not show it.

slides.narration: In the presence of a peroxide, hydrogen bromide adds to propene in the opposite sense, and the main product is one bromopropane. The peroxide produces bromine atoms, which are radicals. The bromine atom adds first, to the end carbon, to give the more stable secondary radical. This radical takes a hydrogen from hydrogen bromide, forming the product and a new bromine atom. This effect is seen only with hydrogen bromide.

slides.heading: Worked example: with and without peroxide
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give the major product when 2-methylpropene reacts with HBr (a) in the dark, without peroxide, (b) in the presence of benzoyl peroxide.

**Solution.** (a) Markownikoff: H adds to CH₂, Br to the carbon with no H: $\ce{(CH3)2C=CH2 + HBr -> (CH3)3CBr}$, **2-bromo-2-methylpropane** (via the tertiary carbocation). (b) Peroxide effect: Br adds to CH₂ and H to the other carbon: **1-bromo-2-methylpropane**, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br.

visual.alt: Table comparing the products of addition of HBr to 2-methylpropene with and without peroxide

slides.narration: Compare the two conditions. Without a peroxide, the ionic mechanism applies. The hydrogen goes to the carbon with more hydrogens, and the bromine ends up on the carbon with none, giving two bromo two methylpropane through a tertiary carbocation. With a peroxide, the radical mechanism applies, bromine adds to the end carbon, and the product is one bromo two methylpropane.

slides.heading: Addition of sulphuric acid and water
slides.body_md: Cold conc. H₂SO₄ adds to ethene to give **ethyl hydrogensulphate**, which on warming with water gives **ethanol**: $\ce{CH2=CH2 + H2SO4 -> CH3CH2OSO3H}$, then $\ce{CH3CH2OSO3H + H2O -> CH3CH2OH + H2SO4}$. Propene follows Markownikoff's rule and gives **propan-2-ol**. Direct **hydration** with water and an acid catalyst (dilute H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄) does the same.

visual.alt: Acid-catalysed hydration of propene gives propan-2-ol following Markownikoff rule
visual.caption: Hydration of propene

slides.narration: Concentrated sulphuric acid adds to ethene in the cold to give ethyl hydrogensulphate. When this is warmed with water it hydrolyses to ethanol and sulphuric acid is regenerated. Propene follows Markownikoff rule, so the hydrogensulphate group goes to the middle carbon and the final product is propan two ol. Alkenes can also be hydrated directly with water and an acid catalyst.

slides.heading: Quick check: hydration of an alkene
slides.body_md: Add H and OH according to Markownikoff's rule.
slides.narration: Quick check. In hydration the hydroxyl group acts as the negative part of the reagent.

slides.heading: Oxidation: combustion and potassium permanganate
slides.body_md: **Combustion:** $\ce{C2H4 + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 2H2O}$ (a luminous, smoky flame). **Cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent):** adds two OH groups, giving a **diol**; the purple colour disappears and a brown precipitate of MnO₂ forms (test for unsaturation). **Hot concentrated KMnO₄** cleaves C=C: =CH₂ → CO₂ + H₂O, =CHR → RCOOH, =CR₂ → R₂C=O.

visual.alt: Table of products of oxidation of four alkenes with cold dilute alkaline potassium permanganate and with hot potassium permanganate

slides.narration: Alkenes burn with a luminous smoky flame to give carbon dioxide and water. With cold dilute alkaline potassium permanganate, called Baeyer reagent, two hydroxyl groups add across the double bond to give a diol; the purple colour disappears and a brown precipitate forms. With hot concentrated permanganate the double bond is broken, and the products are carbon dioxide, carboxylic acids or ketones.

slides.narration: In ozonolysis, ozone adds to the double bond to form an unstable compound called an ozonide. Treatment with zinc and water breaks it into two carbonyl compounds. The double bond is cut, and each carbon that was part of it now carries a double bonded oxygen. A carbon with two hydrogens gives methanal, one with one hydrogen gives an aldehyde, and one with none gives a ketone.

slides.heading: Worked example: finding an alkene from its bromine uptake
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An alkene of mass 2.10 g reacts completely with 4.00 g of bromine (Br₂ = 160 g mol⁻¹). Find its molecular formula.

**Solution.** 1 mol of alkene takes 1 mol of Br₂. n(Br₂) = 4.00 ÷ 160 = 0.0250 mol, so M(alkene) = 2.10 ÷ 0.0250 = 84 g mol⁻¹. For CₙH₂ₙ, 14n = 84, so n = 6: **C₆H₁₂** (a hexene).

visual.alt: Table of the amount of bromine, the molar mass of the alkene and the number of carbon atoms

slides.narration: One mole of an alkene adds one mole of bromine, so the moles of bromine equal the moles of alkene. Four grams of bromine is point zero two five moles, since bromine has a molar mass of one hundred and sixty. Dividing the mass of the alkene by this gives a molar mass of eighty four. For C n H two n the molar mass is fourteen n, so n is six. The alkene is a hexene.

slides.heading: Polymerisation
slides.body_md: **Polymerisation** joins many alkene molecules (monomers) into a long chain. Ethene gives **polythene** (polyethylene): $n\,\text{CH}_2\text{=CH}_2 \rightarrow (\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–})_n$. High pressure (1000–2000 atm, 350–570 K, trace O₂) gives low-density polythene; a Ziegler–Natta catalyst at lower pressure gives high-density polythene. Propene gives **polypropene**.

visual.alt: Table of monomers, polymers, conditions and uses for polythene and polypropene

slides.narration: Polymerisation joins thousands of small molecules into one long chain. Ethene polymerises to polythene. At very high pressure and about five hundred kelvin, with a trace of oxygen, it forms the low density type used for bags and films. With a Ziegler Natta catalyst at lower pressure it forms the high density type used for bottles and pipes. Propene gives polypropene, used for ropes and crates.

slides.heading: Uses of alkenes
slides.body_md: Ethene is the most important organic raw material: **polythene, ethanol, ethane-1,2-diol (antifreeze), ethylene oxide, PVC** and **ripening of fruits**. Propene gives polypropene, propan-2-ol and acrylonitrile. Alkenes are also the starting materials for many detergents, solvents and synthetic fibres.

rows: Polythene, ethanol, antifreeze, PVC, ripening fruit

visual.alt: Table of the main uses of ethene, propene and butenes

slides.narration: Ethene is the most important raw material of the organic chemical industry. It is converted into polythene, ethanol, the antifreeze ethane one two diol, and the monomer for polyvinyl chloride. It is also used to ripen fruit artificially. Propene is the source of polypropene and propan two ol. Many solvents, detergents and synthetic fibres begin with alkenes.

notes.title: Alkenes — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Nomenclature and the structure of the double bond
sections.body_md: **Alkenes** are unsaturated hydrocarbons with one C=C bond; general formula **CₙH₂ₙ**. **Naming:** longest chain containing the double bond; change **-ane to -ene**; number to give the double bond the **lowest locant** (but-1-ene, pent-2-ene, 2-methylbut-2-ene). **Structure of ethene:** each carbon is **sp² hybridised**; three sp² orbitals form σ bonds in one plane (H–C–H 117°, H–C=C 121.5°); the unhybridised **p orbitals** overlap sideways to form the **π bond** above and below the plane. **C=C 134 pm** (C–C 154 pm); C₂H₄ has 5 σ bonds and 1 π bond. The π bond is weaker and exposed, so alkenes are reactive, and it prevents rotation about C=C.

key_terms.definition_md: An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing one carbon–carbon double bond.
A bond formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals; its electron density lies above and below the bond axis.

sections.heading: 2. Isomerism in alkenes
sections.body_md: **Chain isomerism** (but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene), **position isomerism** (but-1-ene and but-2-ene) and **geometrical isomerism** (cis and trans), which needs restricted rotation and **two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon**. C₄H₈ has **3 alkenes** (4 stereoisomers); C₅H₁₀ has **5 alkenes** (6 stereoisomers). Alkenes are **functional isomers of cycloalkanes** (C₄H₈ and cyclobutane).

key_terms.definition_md: Stereoisomerism due to restricted rotation about a double bond: cis (like groups on the same side) and trans (opposite sides).

sections.heading: 3. Preparation of alkenes
sections.body_md: **Dehydration of alcohols:** conc. H₂SO₄ at **443 K** (or Al₂O₃ at 623 K): CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O; ease 3° > 2° > 1°; at 413 K with excess alcohol an ether forms. **Dehydrohalogenation:** alcoholic KOH, heat. **Saytzeff's rule:** the **more substituted** (more stable) alkene is the major product (2-bromobutane gives mainly but-2-ene). **Vicinal dihalides:** CH₂BrCH₂Br + Zn → CH₂=CH₂ + ZnBr₂. **Kolbe's method:** electrolysis of aqueous potassium succinate gives ethene at the anode (with CO₂), H₂ and KOH at the cathode. **From alkynes:** H₂ with **Lindlar's catalyst** (Pd/CaCO₃, poisoned) gives the **cis** alkene; **Na in liquid NH₃** gives the **trans** alkene.

key_terms.definition_md: In an elimination, the more substituted (more stable) alkene is the major product.
Palladium on calcium carbonate, partly poisoned, used to stop the reduction of an alkyne at the cis alkene.

sections.heading: 4. Physical properties
sections.body_md: Alkenes are non-polar or weakly polar: **insoluble in water**, soluble in organic solvents, **less dense than water**. C₂–C₄ are gases, C₅ onwards liquids; boiling points are close to those of the alkanes with the same number of carbons (pent-1-ene 30.0 °C, pentane 36.1 °C) and rise with chain length. **cis versus trans:** the cis isomer is slightly polar (net dipole), so it has the **higher boiling point** (cis-but-2-ene 3.7 °C, trans 0.9 °C; cis-1,2-dichloroethene 1.9 D, 60.3 °C, trans 0 D, 47.5 °C); the symmetrical trans isomer has the **higher melting point** (−105.5 °C against −138.9 °C).

key_terms.definition_md: A measure of the polarity of a molecule: the vector sum of its bond dipoles.

sections.heading: 5. Addition reactions and the mechanism
sections.body_md: **H₂** (Ni, 473 K; Pt or Pd at room temperature) gives the alkane. **Br₂ in CCl₄** gives a vicinal dibromide and the red-brown colour is lost (test). **HX:** Markownikoff's rule — *the negative part adds to the carbon with fewer hydrogens*; propene + HBr gives 2-bromopropane. **H₂SO₄** gives an alkyl hydrogensulphate, hydrolysed by water to the alcohol; **water** with an acid catalyst also gives the alcohol (propene gives propan-2-ol). **Electrophilic addition:** step 1 (slow) the π electrons attack H⁺, forming a carbocation; step 2 (fast) the nucleophile attacks. Carbocation stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl (+I effect, hyperconjugation), which explains Markownikoff's rule.

key_terms.definition_md: When HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the negative part goes to the carbon with fewer hydrogens.
A species that accepts an electron pair; it attacks regions of high electron density such as C=C.
The delocalisation of electrons from adjacent C–H bonds into an empty p orbital, stabilising a carbocation.

sections.heading: 6. Peroxide effect
sections.body_md: In the presence of a peroxide (e.g. benzoyl peroxide), **HBr only** adds to propene to give **1-bromopropane** (anti-Markownikoff). The mechanism is a **free-radical chain**: ROOR → 2RO•; RO• + HBr → ROH + Br•; Br• adds to C-1 to give the more stable **secondary radical**; this takes H from HBr to give the product and Br•. HCl does not show the effect (H–Cl 431 kJ mol⁻¹ is too strong) nor does HI (H–I 299 kJ mol⁻¹; I• does not add readily). H–Br is 366 kJ mol⁻¹.

sections.heading: 7. Oxidation, ozonolysis, polymerisation and uses
sections.body_md: **Combustion:** C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O (luminous, smoky flame). **Cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's test):** adds two OH groups to give a **diol** (ethane-1,2-diol from ethene); purple colour lost and brown MnO₂ forms. **Hot concentrated KMnO₄** cleaves C=C: =CH₂ → CO₂ + H₂O; =CHR → RCOOH; =CR₂ → ketone. **Ozonolysis** (O₃, then Zn/H₂O): the C=C is cut and each carbon becomes C=O: =CH₂ → methanal, =CHR → aldehyde, =CR₂ → ketone; to find an alkene, join the carbonyl carbons by C=C. **Polymerisation:** n CH₂=CH₂ → (–CH₂–CH₂–)ₙ, polythene (high pressure, trace O₂: low density; Ziegler–Natta: high density); propene gives polypropene. **Uses:** polymers, ethanol, antifreeze, PVC, ripening of fruits.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Numbering the chain from the end nearer a substituent instead of giving the double bond the lowest locant.
- Applying Markownikoff's rule to the peroxide reaction (it is reversed), or claiming the peroxide effect for HCl and HI.
- Saying that Lindlar's catalyst gives the trans alkene (it gives cis; Na/NH₃ gives trans).
- Writing that cold alkaline KMnO₄ cleaves the double bond (it gives a diol; hot KMnO₄ cleaves).
- Forgetting that the cis isomer has the higher boiling point but the trans isomer the higher melting point.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Mechanisms: one mark for each step with the correct intermediate (carbocation or radical), one for the product, and one for the reason (stability).
- Preparations: equation with the correct reagent and conditions.
- Ozonolysis: products from cutting at C=C; structure from joining the carbonyl carbons.
- Calculations: balanced equation, moles, answer with the unit.

questions.stem_md: A flavour chemist draws the structure CH₃CH(CH₃)CH=CHCH₂CH₃ for a compound isolated from a plant oil. Its IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: The longest chain containing C=C has 6 carbons. The double bond is at C-3 from either end, so the tie is broken by the methyl group, which gets the lower locant 2: 2-methylhex-3-ene, option (c). Option (a) numbers from the wrong end, (b) gives the double bond a higher locant and (d) does not use the longest chain.

questions.stem_md: In a molecule of propene, CH₃–CH=CH₂, the hybridisation of the three carbon atoms, taken from the CH₃ end, is:
questions.solution_md: The CH₃ carbon has four σ bonds (sp³); each doubly bonded carbon has three σ bonds and one π bond (sp²). The order is sp³, sp², sp² — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The numbers of σ bonds and π bonds in one molecule of propene, C₃H₆, are respectively:
questions.solution_md: Propene has 2 C–C bonds (one of them double) and 6 C–H bonds. All 8 links give σ bonds and the C=C adds one π bond, so 8 σ and 1 π — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student counts every open-chain structural isomer of C₅H₁₀ that contains one carbon–carbon double bond, ignoring cis–trans forms. The number is:
questions.solution_md: The isomers are pent-1-ene, pent-2-ene, 2-methylbut-1-ene, 3-methylbut-1-ene and 2-methylbut-2-ene: 5 in all — option (d). Counting the cis and trans forms of pent-2-ene separately would give 6 (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these bromo-compounds exists as a pair of cis–trans isomers?
questions.solution_md: Cis–trans isomerism needs two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon. In CH₃CH=CHBr each carbon has H and a different group — option (d). The others have two identical groups (H, H; CH₃, CH₃; Br, Br) on one carbon (a, b, c).

questions.stem_md: Ethanol is heated with an excess of concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K. The main organic product is:
questions.solution_md: At 443 K with excess acid, ethanol loses water from adjacent carbons to give ethene, option (c). Ethoxyethane (a) forms at about 413 K with excess alcohol.

questions.stem_md: A student heats 2-bromo-3-methylbutane with alcoholic potassium hydroxide. According to Saytzeff's rule, the major product is:
questions.solution_md: The carbon with Br is C-2; its β-carbons are C-1 (3 H) and C-3 (1 H). Removing the C-3 hydrogen gives the more substituted alkene, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, 2-methylbut-2-ene — option (c). Loss from C-1 gives 3-methylbut-1-ene (a); (b) has the wrong skeleton and (d) is a substitution product that alcoholic KOH does not favour.

questions.stem_md: A sample of 1,2-dibromopropane is warmed with zinc dust in ethanol. The organic product is:
questions.solution_md: Zinc removes the two bromine atoms from adjacent carbons as ZnBr₂ and leaves a C=C bond: propene — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A concentrated aqueous solution of potassium succinate, KOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOK, is electrolysed. The hydrocarbon liberated at the anode is:
questions.solution_md: Each carboxylate group is lost as CO₂ and the two remaining CH₂ carbons join by a double bond: ⁻OOC–CH₂–CH₂–COO⁻ gives CH₂=CH₂ + 2CO₂ + 2e⁻. The product is ethene — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Hex-2-yne is treated with sodium in liquid ammonia. The main product is:
questions.solution_md: Sodium in liquid ammonia reduces an alkyne to the trans alkene by anti addition of hydrogen: trans-hex-2-ene — option (b). The cis isomer (a) needs H₂/Lindlar catalyst; hexane (c) would need full hydrogenation.

questions.stem_md: Four alcohols are warmed with the same concentrated acid under identical conditions. The one that dehydrates most easily is:
questions.solution_md: The ease of dehydration follows carbocation stability: tertiary > secondary > primary. 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary — option (d); butan-2-ol (b) is secondary and butan-1-ol and ethanol (a, c) are primary.

questions.stem_md: cis-But-2-ene boils at 277 K and trans-but-2-ene at 274 K. The main reason why the cis isomer has the higher boiling point is that it:

options.text_md: is more symmetrical and packs better in the liquid
has a small net dipole moment, so it has extra dipole–dipole attraction

questions.solution_md: The two isomers have the same molar mass (a). In the cis form the two C–CH₃ bond dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule is slightly polar and has extra dipole–dipole attraction; in the trans form they cancel — option (d). Symmetry (b) raises the melting point, not the boiling point, and there is no hydrogen bonding (c).

questions.stem_md: Of these four chlorine-containing alkenes, the one with a zero dipole moment is:
questions.solution_md: In the trans isomer the two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, giving zero net dipole moment — option (b). The cis isomer (about 1.9 D), chloroethene and 1,1-dichloroethene all have a net dipole.

questions.stem_md: But-1-ene reacts with hydrogen chloride in the absence of peroxides. The major product is:
questions.solution_md: By Markownikoff's rule H goes to C-1 (which has more hydrogens) and Cl to C-2, via the secondary carbocation: CH₃CH₂CHClCH₃, 2-chlorobutane — option (a). Option (b) is the anti-Markownikoff product; (c) and (d) need other reagents.

questions.stem_md: Propene is passed into dilute sulphuric acid and the mixture is warmed. The main product is:
questions.solution_md: Acid-catalysed hydration follows Markownikoff's rule: H adds to C-1 and OH to C-2, giving CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, propan-2-ol — option (a). Propan-1-ol (b) would be the anti-Markownikoff product; (c) needs oxidising conditions and (d) is a ketone.

questions.stem_md: In the acid-catalysed hydration of 2-methylpropene, the carbocation formed in the first step is:
questions.solution_md: H⁺ adds to the CH₂ carbon, leaving the positive charge on the carbon bearing two methyl groups: the tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺ — option (a). Adding H⁺ to the other carbon would give the less stable primary cation (b).

questions.stem_md: But-1-ene reacts with hydrogen bromide in the presence of benzoyl peroxide. The major product is:
questions.solution_md: With a peroxide, HBr adds by a free-radical chain: Br• attacks C-1 to give the more stable secondary radical, so Br ends on C-1 (anti-Markownikoff): 1-bromobutane — option (b). Option (a) is the product without peroxide.

questions.stem_md: Ethene gas is bubbled into a red-brown solution of bromine in tetrachloromethane. The observation and the organic product are:
questions.solution_md: Bromine adds across the C=C bond, so its colour is lost and colourless 1,2-dibromoethane forms — option (b). This is the usual test for unsaturation.

questions.stem_md: The peroxide effect is not observed with hydrogen chloride mainly because:

options.text_md: chlorine radicals cannot add to a C=C bond at all
chlorine is less electronegative than bromine
the H–Cl bond is too strong, so the step in which the carbon radical takes hydrogen from HCl is unfavourable
peroxides react with HCl and are used up

questions.solution_md: The radical chain needs the carbon radical to abstract H from HX. The H–Cl bond (431 kJ mol⁻¹) is much stronger than H–Br (366 kJ mol⁻¹), so this step is energetically unfavourable and the chain does not propagate — option (c). Chlorine radicals do add to alkenes (a), electronegativity (b) is not the issue, and peroxides are not consumed by HCl (d).

questions.stem_md: Propene is shaken with cold, dilute, alkaline potassium permanganate solution. The organic product is:
questions.solution_md: Cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ adds two OH groups across the C=C bond (Baeyer's test): CH₃CH(OH)CH₂OH, propane-1,2-diol — option (d). Ethanoic acid (b) and propanone (c) are cleavage products formed only with hot concentrated reagent.

questions.stem_md: But-2-ene is boiled with hot, concentrated acidified potassium permanganate. The organic product is:
questions.solution_md: Hot KMnO₄ cleaves the C=C bond and oxidises each =CHCH₃ fragment to CH₃COOH. Two molecules of ethanoic acid form — option (a). Ethanal (b) would be the ozonolysis product; the diol (c) forms with the cold reagent.

questions.stem_md: An alkene is treated with ozone and the ozonide is decomposed with zinc and water. The only organic product is propanone. The alkene is:
questions.solution_md: Propanone, (CH₃)₂C=O, is the only product, so both ends of the double bond are =C(CH₃)₂. Joining two such carbons gives (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂, 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene — option (c). The others would give propanone plus another compound (a, b) or only ethanal (d).

questions.stem_md: The repeating unit in the polymer formed from propene is:
questions.solution_md: Opening the double bond of CH₃CH=CH₂ gives the unit –CH(CH₃)–CH₂–, repeated n times in polypropene — option (b). Option (a) is the unit of polythene.

questions.stem_md: Ethene burns completely in oxygen. At the same temperature and pressure, the volume of oxygen needed for 2.4 L of ethene is:
questions.solution_md: C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O. By Gay-Lussac's law the volumes of gases are in the ratio of the coefficients, so $V(\text{O}_2) = 3 \times 2.4 = 7.2\ \text{L}$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Using curved arrows described in words, write the mechanism for the addition of hydrogen bromide to 2-methylpropene and name the carbocation and the product.

questions.stem_md: Explain, with equations for the steps, how the addition of HBr to propene in the presence of benzoyl peroxide gives 1-bromopropane and not 2-bromopropane.

answer.model_answer_md: The peroxide splits into radicals which abstract H from HBr to give Br•. questions.stem_md: Explain why a tertiary carbocation is more stable than a primary carbocation, using the ideas of inductive effect and hyperconjugation, and say how this controls the product of the addition of HBr to propene.

So the stability order is tertiary > secondary > primary. In propene, H⁺ adds to give the secondary carbocation rather than the primary one, so Br⁻ ends on C-2 and 2-bromopropane is the main product.

questions.stem_md: A sample of 5.60 L of ethene, measured at STP, is burnt completely in air. Write the balanced equation and calculate the volume of oxygen consumed at STP and the mass of carbon dioxide formed. (C = 12, O = 16; molar volume 22.4 L)
